characters.display: Knight of Fahnenberg / Baron von Fahnenberg

P1.text: It appears, dear Franziska, that the hardships of the road have affected you more than you will acknowledge. Generally so kind to others, you have been very often out of humour during the journey, and particularly with regard to your humble servant and cousin, who would gladly bear a double or treble share of the discomforts, if he could thereby save you from the smallest of them.

P2.text: I should like to scold you well, Franziska, for always plaguing your poor Cousin Franz in this shameful way; he who loves you so truly, and who, whatever you may say, will one day be your husband.

P3.text: My husband! I must either completely alter my ideas, or he his whole self, before that takes place. No, Bertha! I know that this is my father's darling wish, and I do not deny the good qualities Cousin Franz may have, or really has, since I see you are making a face; but to marry an effeminate man — never!

P4.text: Effeminate! you do him great injustice. Just because instead of going off to the Turkish war, where little honour was to be gained, he attended to your father's advice, and stayed at home, to bring his neglected estate into order, which he accomplished with care and prudence; and because he does not represent this howling wind as a mild zephyr — for reasons such as these you are pleased to call him effeminate

P6.text: Say what you will, it is so. Bold, aspiring, even despotic, must be the man who is to gain my heart; these soft, patient, and thoughtful natures are utterly distasteful to me. Is Franz capable of deep sympathy, either in joy or sorrow? He is always the same — always quiet, soft and tiresome.

P7.text: He has a warm heart, and is not without genius.

P8.text: A warm heart! that may be but I would rather be tyrannized over, and kept under a little by my future husband, than be loved in such a wearisome manner. You say he has genius, too. I will not exactly contradict you, since that would be unpolite, but it is not easily discovered. But even allowing you are right in both statements, still the man who does not bring these qualities into action is a despicable creature. A man may do many foolish things, he may even be a little wicked now and then, provided it is in nothing dishonourable; and one can forgive him, if he is only acting on some fixed theory for some special object. There is, for instance, your own faithful admirer, the Castellan of Glogau, Knight of Woislaw; he loves you most truly, and is now quite in a position to enable you to marry comfortably. The brave man has lost his right hand — reason enough for remaining seated behind the stove, or near the spinning-wheel of his Bertha; but what does he do? — He goes off to the war in Turkey; he fights for a noble thought —

P9.text: And runs the chance of getting his other hand chopped off, and another great scar across his face.

P10.text: Leaves his lady-love to weep and pine a little, but returns with fame, marries, and is all the more honoured and admired! This is done by a man of forty, a rough warrior, not bred at court, a soldier who has nothing but his cloak and sword. And Franz — rich, noble — but I will not go on. Not a word more on this detested point, if you love me, Bertha.

P11.text: This awful wind is so powerful, you say, that we must make a detour to avoid its full force.

P12.text: Those who have never personally felt the Boreas storming over the country between Sessano and Triest, can have no conception of the reality. As soon as it commences, the snow is blown in thick long columns along the ground. That is nothing to what follows. These columns become higher and higher, as the wind rises, and continue to do so until you see nothing but snow above, below, and on every side — unless, indeed, sometimes, when sand and gravel are mixed with the snow, and at length it is impossible to open your eyes at all. Your only plan for safety is to wrap your cloak around you, and lie down flat on the ground. If your home were but a few hundred yards off, you might lose your life in the attempt to reach it.

P13.text: Well, then, we owe you thanks, old Kumpan, we owe you thanks for taking us this round, as we shall thus be enabled to reach our destination without danger.

P14.text: You may feel sure of that, noble sir. By midnight we shall have arrived, and that without any danger by the way, if —

P15.text: It appears to me we must be in the neighbourhood of some village, for between the gusts of the storm I hear a dog howling.

P16.text: It is no dog, it is no dog! For miles around there is no human dwelling; and except in the castle of Klatka, which indeed lies in the neighbourhood, but has been deserted for more than a century, probably no one has lived here since the creation. — But there again well, if I wasn't sure of it from the first.

P17.text: That howling seems to fidget you, old Kumpan.

P18.text: That howling comes from no dogs. Those are reed-wolves; they may be on our track; and it would be as well if the gentlemen looked to their firearms.

P20.text: At the edge of this wood, there lies a lake about a mile long, whose banks are covered with reeds. In these a number of wolves have taken up their quarters, and feed on wild birds, fish and such like. They are shy in the summer-time, and a boy of twelve might scare them; but when the birds migrate, and the fish ate frozen up, they. prowl about at night, and then they are dangerous. They are worst, however, when Boreas rages, for then it is just as if the fiend himself possessed them: they are so mad and fierce that man and beast become alike their victims; and a party of them have been known even to attack the ferocious bears of these mountains, and, what is more, to come off victorious.

P21.text: We must keep dose to the litter; the wolves are very near us.

P22.text: Then we shall have an adventure — some little variety!

P23.text: How can you talk so foolishly?

P24.text: Are we not under manly protection? Is not Cousin Franz on our side?

P25.text: See, there is a light gleaming among the twigs; and there is another, there must be people close to us.

P26.text: No, no. Shut up the door, ladies. Keep close together, gentlemen. It is the eyes of wolves you see sparkling there.

P27.text: I will fire on the beasts, and teach them to keep their distance.

P28.text: Hold, hold, Sir Baron! You would bring such a host together by the report, that, encouraged by numbers, they would be sure to make the first assault. However, keep your arms in readiness, and if an old she-wolf springs out — for these always lead the attack — take good aim and kill her, for then there must be no further hesitation.

P30.text: Now, forward! Forward without a moment's delay! We have not above five minutes' time. The beasts will tear their wounded comrade to pieces, and, if they are very hungry, partially devour her. We shall, in the meantime, gain a little start, and it is not more than an hour's ride to the end of the forest. There — do you see — these are the towers of Klatka between the trees — out there where the moon is rising, and from that point the wood becomes less dense.

P31.text: There they are again and fiercer and more numerous than before.

P32.text: We are in great danger, noble sir. The wolves will very soon make a general attack. There will then be only one way of escape: leaving the mules to their fate, and taking the young ladies on your horses.

P33.text: That would be all very well, if I had not thought of a better plan. Here is the ruined castle; we can surely reach that, and then, blocking up the gates, we must just await the morning.

P34.text: Here? In the ruins of Klatka? — Not for all the wolves in the world! Even by daylight no one likes to approach the place, and, now, by night! — The castle, Sir Knight, has a bad name.

P37.text: Stuff and nonsense! Forward to the ruins; there is not a moment to be lost.

P40.text: Did you know the man who met us near the ruins, and who freed us from our four-footed pursuers in such a miraculous way?

P41.text: Do I know him? No, noble sir; I never saw him before.

P42.text: He looked like a soldier, and was armed. Is the castle, then, inhabited?

P43.text: Not for the last hundred years. It was dismantled because the possessor in those days had iniquitous dealings with some Turkish-Sclavonian hordes, who had advanced as far as this; or rather he is said to have had such, for he might have been as upright and good a man as ever ate cheese fried in butter.

P44.text: And who is now the possessor of the ruins and of these woods?

P45.text: Who but yourself, noble sir? For more than two hours we have been on your estate, and we shall soon reach the end of the wood.

P46.text: We hear and see nothing more of the wolves. Even their howling has ceased. The adventure with the stranger still remains to me inexplicable, even if one were to suppose him a huntsman—

P47.text: Yes, yes; that is most likely what he is. The brave good man, who came so opportunely to our assistance, must have been a huntsman Oh, there are many powerful woodsmen in this neighbourhood! Heaven be praised! There is the end of the wood, and in a short hour we shall be safely housed.

P48.text: I have it. I wonder we never thought before of going to view by day the spot where we fell in with our night-adventure with wolves and the Mysterious Stranger.

P49.text: You mean a visit to the ruins — what were they called?

P50.text: Castle Klatka. Oh, we really must ride there! It will be so charming to go over again by daylight, and in safety, the ground where we had such a dreadful fright.

P51.text: Bring round the horses,and tell the steward to come to me immediately.

P52.text: We intend taking a ride to Klatka, we had an adventure there on our road.

P54.text: And what do you say about it?

P55.text: I really don't know what to say, I was a youth of twenty when I first came to this castle, and now my hair is grey; half a century has elapsed during that time. Hundreds of times my duty has called me into the neighbourhood of those ruins, but never have I seen the Fiend of Klatka.

P56.text: What do you say? Whom do you call by that name?

P57.text: Why, people call by that name the ghost or spirit who is supposed to haunt the ruins. They say he only shows himself on moonlight nights —

P58.text: That is quite natural. Ghosts can never bear the light of day; and if the moon did not shine, how could the ghost be seen? for it is not supposed that any one for a mere freak would visit the ruins by torch-light.

P59.text: There are some credulous people who pretend to have seen this ghost. Huntsmen and wood-cutters say they have met him by the large oak on the cross-path. That, noble sir, is supposed to be the spot he inclines most to haunt, for the tree was planted in remembrance of the man who fell there.

P61.text: The last owner of the castle, which at that time was a sort of robber's den, and the headquarters of all depredators in the neighbourhood,.They say this man was of superhuman strength, and was feared not only on account of his passionate temper, but of his treaties with the Turkish hordes. Any young woman, too, in the neighbourhood to whom he took a fancy, was carried off to his tower and never heard of more. When the measure of his iniquity was full, the whole neighbourhood rose in a mass, besieged his stronghold, and at length he was slain on the spot where the huge oak-tree now stands.

P62.text: I wonder they did not burn the whole castle, so as to erase the very memory of it.

P63.text: It was a dependency of the church, and that saved it. Your great-grandfather afterwards took possession of it, for it had fine lands attached. As the Knight of Klatka was of good family, a monument was erected to him in the church, which now lies as much in ruin as the castle itself.

P64.text: Oh, let us set off at once! Nothing shall prevent my visiting so interesting a spot. The imprisoned damsels who never reappeared, the storming of the tower, the death of the knight, the nightly wanderings of his spirit round the old oak, and, lastly, our own adventure, all draw me thither with an indescribable curiosity.

P65.text: That must be the monument of the knight whose ghost is said to haunt these ruins.

P66.text: What a pity he is not represented in the same way as the others — I should so like to have known what he was like!

P67.text: Oh, there is the family vault, with steps leading down to it, and the sun is lighting it up through a crevice.

P68.text: If I am not mistaken, we have met before.

P69.text: You released us in an almost miraculous manner, from the power of those dreadful wolves. Am I wrong in supposing it is to you we are indebted for that great service?

P70.text: The beasts are afraid of me.

P71.text: Then you are probably a huntsman, and wage war against the fierce brutes.

P72.text: Who is not either the pursuer or the pursued? All persecute or are persecuted, and Fate persecutes all.

P73.text: Do you live in these ruins?

P74.text: Yes; but not to the destruction of your game, as you may fear, Knight of Fahnenberg. Be quite assured of your property shall remain untouched —

P75.text: Oh! my father did not mean that. Unfortunate events and sad experiences have, no doubt, induced you to take up your abode in these ruins, of which my father would by no means dispossess you.

P76.text: Your father is very good, if that is what he meant, but people of my sort are rather difficult to turn out.

P77.text: You must live very uncomfortably here.

P78.text: My dwelling is not exactly uncomfortable, only somewhat small, still quite suitable for quiet people. I am not, however, always quiet; I sometimes pine to quit the narrow space, and then I dash away through forest and field, over hill and dale; and the time when I must return to my little dwelling always comes too soon for me.

P79.text: As you now and then leave your dwelling. I would invite you to visit us, if I knew —

P80.text: That I was in a station to admit of your doing so. I lament that I am not able to give you particulars on this point — some difficulties stand in the way: be assured, however, that I am a knight, and of at least as ancient a family as yourself.

P81.text: Then you must not refuse our request. You must come and visit us.

P82.text: I am no boon-companion, and on that account few have invited me of late, besides, I generally remain at home during the day; that is my time for rest. I belong, you must know, to that class of persons who turn day into night, and night into day, and who love everything uncommon and peculiar

P83.text: Really? So do I! And for that reason, you must visit us. Now, I suppose you have just risen, and you are taking your morning airing. Well, since the moon is your sun, pray pay a frequent visit to our castle by the light of its rays. I think we shall agree very well, and that it will be very nice for us to be acquainted.

P84.text: You wish it? — You press the invitation?

P85.text: To be sure, for otherwise you will not come.

P86.text: Well, then, come I will! If my company does not please you at any time, you will have yourself to blame for an acquaintance with one who seldom forces himself, but is difficult to shake off.

P87.text: Pardon me, Sir Knight, that I come, if not uninvited, at least unannounced; there was no one in the ante-chamber to do me that service.

P88.text: For a long time past, I have accustomed myself never to eat at night. My digestion is quite unused to solids, and indeed would scarcely confront them. I live entirely on liquids.

P89.text: Oh, then, we can empty a bumper of Rhine-wine together.

P90.text: Thanks; but I neither drink wine nor any cold beverage.

P91.text: Then I will order you a cup of hippocras, it shall be ready immediately.

P92.text: Many thanks, fair lady; not at present. But if I refuse the beverage you offer me now, you may be assured that as soon as I require it — perhaps very soon — I will request that, or some other of you.

P93.text: It is now many weeks since we first became acquainted with you; we then had to thank you for a signal service —

P94.text: And I have not yet told you my name, although you would gladly know it. I am called Azzo; and as with the permission of the Knight of Fahnenberg, I live at the castle of Klatka, you can in future call me Azzo von Klatka.

P95.text: I only wonder you do not feel lonely and uncomfortable amongst those old walls. I cannot understand —

P96.text: What my business is there? Oh, about that I will willingly give you some information, since you and the young gentleman there takes such a kindly interest in my person.

P97.text: You see, lady, there are a variety of strange whims in the world. As I have already said, I love what is peculiar and uncommon, at least what would appear so to you. It is wrong in the main to be astonished at anything, for, viewed in one light, all things are alike; even life and death, this side of the grave and the other, have more resemblance than you would imagine. You perhaps consider me rather touched a little in my mind, for taking up my abode with the bat and the owl; but if so, why not consider every hermit and recluse insane? You will tell me that those are holy men. I certainly have no pretension that way; but as they find pleasure in praying and singing psalms, so I amuse myself with hunting. Oh, you can have no idea of the intense pleasure of dashing away in the pale moonlight, on a horse that never tires, over hill and dale, through forest and woodland! I rush among the wolves, which fly at my approach, as you yourself perceived, as though they were puppies fearful of the lash.

P98.text: But still it must be lonely, very lonely for you.

P99.text: So it would by day; but I am then asleep, at night I am merry enough.

P100.text: You hunt in an extraordinary way.

P101.text: Yes; but, nevertheless, I have no communication with robbers, as you seem to imagine.

P102.text: Oh, I beg your pardon; I do not know —

P103.text: What to make of me. You would, therefore, do well to believe just what I tell you, or at least to avoid making conjectures of your own, which will lead to nothing.

P104.text: I understand you: I know how to value your ideas, if no one else does. The humdrum, everyday life of the generality of men is repulsive to you; you have tasted the joys and pleasures of life, at least what are so called, and you have found them tame and hollow. How soon one tires of the things one sees all around! Life consists in change. Only in what is new, uncommon, and peculiar, do the flowers of the spirit bloom and give forth scent. Even pain may become a pleasure if it saves one from the shallow monotony of everyday life — a thing I shall hate till the hour of my death.

P105.text: Right, fair lady — quite right! Remain in this mind: this was always my opinion, and the one from which I have derived the highest reward. I am doubly pleased to have found in you a person who shares my ideas. Oh, if you were a man, you would make me a splendid companion; but even a woman may have fine experiences when once these opinions take root in her, and bring forth action!

P106.text: At least you can let me hear this wonderful dream.

P107.text: Come, tell me, what can possibly prevent you from relating a dream — a mere dream? I might almost think it credible, if the idea were not too horrid, that poor Franz is not very far wrong when he says that the thin, corpse-like, dried-up, old-fashioned stranger has made a greater impression on you than you will allow.

P108.text: Did Franz say so? Then you can tell him he is not mistaken. Yes, the thin, corpse-like, dried-up, whimsical stranger is far more interesting to me than the rosy-checked, well-dressed, polite, and prosy cousin.

P109.text: Strange. I cannot at all comprehend the almost magic influence which this man, so repulsive, exercises over you.

P110.text: Perhaps the very reason I take his part, may be that you are all so prejudiced against him. Yes, it must be so; for that his appearance should please my eyes, is what no one in his senses could imagine. But is it not laughable that I should get out of temper even with you about this stranger? — I can more easily understand it with Franz — and that this unknown should spoil my morning, as he has already spoiled my evening and my night's rest?

P111.text: By that dream, you mean? Now, do tell it to me. You know how I delight in hearing anything of the kind.

P112.text: Well, I will, as a sort of compensation for my peevishness towards you. Now, listen! I had walked up and down my room for a long time; I was excited — out of spirits — I do not know exactly what. It was almost midnight ere I lay down, but I could not sleep. I tossed about, and at length it was only from sheer exhaustion that I dropped off. But what a sleep it was! An inward fear ran through me perpetually. I saw a number of pictures before me, as I used to do in childish sicknesses. I do not know whether I was asleep or half awake. Then I dreamed, but as dearly as if I had been wide awake, that a sort of mist filled the room, and out of it stepped the knight Azzo. He gazed at me for a time, and then letting himself slowly down on one knee, imprinted a kiss on my throat. Long did his lips rest there; and I felt a slight pain, which always went on increasing, until I could bear it no more. With all my strength I tried to force the vision from me, but succeeded only after a long struggle. No doubt I uttered a scream, for that awoke me from my trance. when I came a little to my senses, I felt a sort of superstitious fear creeping over me — how great you may imagine when I tell you that, with my eyes open and awake, it appeared to me as if Azzo's figure were still by my bed, and then disappearing gradually into the mist, vanished at the door!

P113.text: You must have dreamed very heavily, my poor friend. Why, what is that? Just look: how extraordinary — a red streak on your throat!

P114.text: I must have hurt myself by some means in my sleep, and that in some measure will account for my dream.

P115.text: I should not wonder if day had surprised us, whilst listening to your entertaining adventures.

P116.text: I admire the young gentleman's taste. Stories of storm and shipwreck are, indeed, best heard on terra firma, and those of battle and death at a hospitable table or in the chimney-corner. One had then the comfortable feeling of keeping a whole skin, and being in no danger, not even of taking cold.

P117.text: That Azzo's impertinence is unbearable. He becomes daily more rough, unpolite, and presuming. If only on account of Franziska's dream, though of course he cannot help that, I detest him. Now, tonight, not one civil word has he spoken to any one but Franziska, except, perhaps, some casual remark to my uncle.

P118.text: I cannot deny that you are right, Bertha. One may forgive much to a man whom fate had probably made somewhat misanthropical; but he should not overstep the bounds of common politeness. But where on earth is Franz?

P119.text: He cannot have followed the knight Azzo to challenge him?

P120.text: It were better he entered a lion's den to pull his mane! I must follow him instantly.

P121.text: Leave me, foolish boy — leave me; for by that you will see those rays no more if you linger another moment on my path.

P122.text: And I tell you, wretch, that you either give me satisfaction for your repeated insolence, or you die.

P123.text: I warn you for the last time. Now, away — away, boy, from my path, or, by those below us, you are lost!

P124.text: You or I! you or I!

P125.text: Who are thou who darest to rob me of my prey? Is it possible? Can you be —

P126.text: Ask not, thou bloody one! Go, seek thy nourishment! Soon comes thy hour!

P127.text: Ha, now I know! Welcome, blood-brother! I give up to you this worm, and for your sake will not crush him. Farewell; our paths will soon meet again.

P129.text: I am dishonoured, dishonoured for ever!

P130.text: Calm yourself; you could not have conquered.

P131.text: But I will conquer, or perish! I will seek this adventurer in his den, and he or I must fall.

P132.text: You could not hurt him. You would infallibly be the victim.

P133.text: Then show me a way to bring the wretch to judgment. Disgraced as I am, I cannot live.

P134.text: You shall be revenged, and that within twenty-four hours, I hope; but only on two conditions —

P135.text: I agree to them! I will do anything —

P136.text: The first is, that you do nothing, but leave everything in my hands. The second, that you will assist me in persuading Franziska to do what I shall represent to her as absolutely necessary. That young lady's life is in more danger from Azzo than your own!

P137.text: How? What? Franziska's life in danger! and from that man? Tell me, Woislaw, who is this fiend?

P138.text: Not a word will I tell either the young lady or you, until the danger is passed. The smallest indiscretion would ruin everything. No one can act here but Franziska herself, and if she refuses to do so she is irretrievably lost.

P139.text: Speak, and I will help you. I will do all you wish, but I must know —

P140.text: Nothing, absolutely nothing. I must have both you and Franziska yield to me unconditionally. Come now, come to her. You are to be mute on what has passed, and use every effort to induce her to accede to my proposal.

P141.text: Oh, I have been so frightened. I trust all has ended peaceably.

P142.text: Everything is arranged; a couple of words were sufficient to settle the whole affair. But Master Franz was less concerned in it than yourself, fair lady.

P146.text: And you spoke of that to Azzo? Does he, then, know a remedy which he could not tell me himself?

P147.text: The knight Azzo must take part in your cure; but speak to you about it he cannot, unless the remedy is to lose all its efficacy.

P148.text: So it is some secret elixir, as the learned doctors say, who have so long attended me, and through whose means I only grow worse.

P149.text: It is certainly a secret, but is as certainly a cure.

P150.text: So said all, but none has succeeded.

P151.text: You might at least try it.

P152.text: Because your friend proposes it. I have no doubt that you, with nothing ailing you, would take all manner of drugs to please your knight; but with me the inducement is wanting, and therefore also the faith.

P153.text: I did not speak of any medicine.

P154.text: Oh! a magical remedy! I am to be cured 'by sympathy.' Yes, that was it.

P155.text: I do not object to your calling it so, if you like, but you must know, dear lady, that the measures I shall propose must be attended to literally, and according to the strictest directions.

P156.text: And you trust this to me?

P158.text: Well, why do you not proceed? Can you think that I shall fail in courage?

P159.text: Courage is certainly necessary for the success of my plan, and it is because I give you credit for a large share of that virtue, I venture to propose it at all, although for the real harmlessness of the remedy I will answer with my life, provided you follow my directions exactly.

P160.text: Well, tell me the plan, and then I can decide.

P161.text: I can only tell you that when we commence our operations.

P162.text: Do you think I am a child to be sent here, there, and everywhere, without a reason?

P163.text: You did me great injustice, dear lady, if you thought for a moment I would propose anything disagreeable to you, unless demanded by the sternest necessity, and yet I can only repeat my former words.

P164.text: Then I will not do it, I have already tried so much, and all ineffectually.

P165.text: I give you my honour as a knight, that your cure is certain, but — you must pledge yourself solemnly and unconditionally to do implicitly what I shall direct.

P166.text: Oh, I implore you to consent, Franziska. Our friend would not propose anything unnecessary.

P167.text: And let me join my entreaties to Bertha's.

P168.text: How strange you all are! You make such a secret of that which I must know if I am to accomplish it, and then you declare so positively that I shall recover, when my own feelings tell me it is quite hopeless.

P169.text: I repeat, that I will answer for the result, on the condition I mentioned before, and that you have courage to carry out what you commence.

P170.text: Ha! Now I understand; this, after all, is the only thing which appears doubtful to you. Well, to show you that our sex are neither wanting in the will nor in the power to accomplish deeds of daring, I give my consent.

P171.text: Our compact is thus sealed. Now say, Sir Knight, how am I to commence this mysterious cure?

P172.text: It commenced when you gave your consent. Now, I have only to request that you will ask no more questions, but hold yourself in readiness to take a ride with me tomorrow an hour before sunset. I also request that you will not mention to your father a word of what has passed.

P174.text: You have made the compact; you are not wanting in resolution; and I will answer for everything else.

P175.text: Well, so let it be. I will follow your directions.

P176.text: On our return you shall know everything; before that, it is quite impossible. Now go, dear lady, and take some rest; you will need strength for to-morrow.

P177.text: In a quarter of an hour, the sun will set, and in another hour the moon will have risen; then all must be accomplished. It will soon be time to commence the work.

P178.text: Then, I should think it was time to entrust me with some idea of what it is.

P179.text: Well, lady, I entreat you, Franziska von Fahnenberg, for your own good, and as you love the father who clings to you with his whole soul, that you will weigh well my words, and that you will not interrupt me with questions which I cannot answer until the work is completed. Your life is in the greatest danger from the illness under which you are labouring; indeed, you are irrecoverably lost if you do not fully carry out what I shall now impart to you. Now, promise me to do implicitly as I shall tell you; I pledge you my knightly word it is nothing against Heaven, or the honour of your house; and, besides, it is the sole means for saving you.

P182.text: Say an Ave; you will have need of it.

P183.text: The moment has arrived! The sun sinks, and before the moon rises, all must be over.

P185.text: You see there that open vault! You must descend. You must go alone; I may not accompany you. When you have reached the vault you will find, close to the entrance, a coffin, on which is placed a small packet. Open this packet, and you will find three long iron nails and a hammer. Then pause for a moment; but when I begin to repeat the Credo in a loud voice, knock with all your might, first one nail, then a second, and then a third, into the lid of the coffin, right up to their heads.

P205.text: It was during my first campaign in Hungary, when I was rendered helpless for some time by this sword-cut of a janizary across my face, and another on my shoulder. I had been taken into the house of a respectable family in a small town. It consisted of the father and mother, and a daughter about twenty years of age. They obtained their living by selling the very good wine of the country, and the taproom was always full of visitors. Although the family were well to do in the world, there seemed to brood over them a continual melancholy, caused by the constant illness of the only daughter, a very pretty and excellent girl. She had always bloomed like a rose, but for some months she had been getting so thin and wasted, and that without any satisfactory reason: they tried every means to restore her, but in vain. As the army had encamped quite in the neighbourhood, of course a number of people of all countries assembled in the tavern. Amongst these there was one man who came every evening, when the moon shone, who struck everybody by the peculiarity of his manners and appearance; he looked dried up and deathlike, and hardly spoke at all; but what he did say was bitter and sarcastic. Most attention was excited towards him by the circumstance, that although he always ordered a cup of the best wine, and now and then raised it to his lips, the cup was always as full after his departure as at first.

P206.text: This all agrees wonderfully with the appearance of Azzo.

It was singular that the girl always complained of a dream, in which the unknown guest worried and plagued her.

P209.text: One evening, an old Sclavonian — who had made many voyages to Turkey and Greece, and had even seen the New World — and I were sitting over our wine, and sat down at the table. The bottle passed quickly between my friend and me, whilst we talked of all manner of things, of our adventures, and of passages in our lives, both horrible and amusing. We went on chatting thus for about an hour, and drank a tolerable quantity of wine. The unknown had remained perfectly silent the whole time, only smiling contemptuously every now and then. He now paid his money, and was going away. All this had quietly worried me — perhaps the wine had got a little into my head —so I said to the stranger: 'Hold, you stony stranger; you have hitherto done nothing but listen, and have not even emptied your cup. Now you shall take your turn in telling us something amusing, and if you do not drink up your wine, it shall produce a quarrel between us.' 'Yes,' said the Sclavonian, 'you must remain; you shall chat and drink, too;' and he grasped — for although no longer young, he was big and very strong — the stranger by the shoulder, to pull him down to his seat again: the latter, however, although as thin as a skeleton, with one movement of his hand flung the Sclavonian to the middle of the room, and half stunned him for a moment. I now approached to hold the stranger back. I caught him by the arm; and although the springs of my iron hand were less powerful than those I have at present, I must have gripped him rather hard in my anger, for after looking grimly at me for a moment, he bent towards me and whispered in my ear: 'Let me go from the gripe of your fist, I see you are my brother, therefore do not hinder me from seeking my bloody nourishment. I am hungry!' Surprised by such words, I let him loose, and almost before I was aware he had left the room. As soon as I had in some degree recovered from my astonishment, I told the Sclavonian what I had heard. He started, evidently alarmed. I asked him to tell me the cause of his fears, and pressed him for an explanation of those extraordinary words. On our way to his lodging, he complied with my request. 'The stranger,' said he, 'is a Vampire!'

They were deceased persons, who had either once served as nourishment to vampires, or who had died in deadly sin, or under excommunication; and that whenever the moon shone, they rose from their graves, and sucked the blood of the living.

"Azzo, as well as the other vampire, mistook its great power for that of a natural one, and concluded I was one of his own species. — You may now imagine, dear lady, how alarmed I was at your appearance when I arrived: all you and Bertha told me increased my anxiety; and when I saw Azzo, I could doubt no longer that he was a vampire. As I learned from your account that a grave with the name Ezzelin von Klatka lay in the neighbourhood, I had no doubt that you might be saved if I could only induce you to assist me. It did not appear to me advisable to impart the whole facts of the case, for your bodily powers were so impaired, that an idea of the horrors before you might have quite unfitted you for the exertion; for this reason, I arranged everything in the manner in which it has taken place.

P217.text: That was what I feared, but fortune has favoured us all through.

P218.text: And what became of the unfortunate girl in Hungary?

P219.text: I know not. That very evening there was an alarm of Turks, and we were ordered off. I never beard anything more of her.

In this way it grew close to midnight. At last I lay down, but could not sleep, and tossed to and fro; finally I fell asleep from sheer exhaustion. But what a sleep it was! An inward terror continually shot through me; I saw a multitude of shapes, such as I used to see in childhood when I lay ill. Even now I do not know whether I was asleep or half awake. Then I dreamed—but so vividly that it seemed I was fully awake—that a mist suddenly filled my room, and out of the mist stepped Knight Azzo. He looked at me for a while, then slowly sank to one knee and pressed a kiss upon my neck. For a long time his lips rested there, and I felt a slight pain which gradually increased and grew more intense until I could bear it no longer. With great effort I tried to push the apparition away from me, but it was only after a long time that I succeeded. I must have cried out in my sleep, for it seemed to me that the cry itself awakened me. As I became more fully awake, I found myself in a state of indescribable terror and agitation; and you can imagine how great it was when I tell you that, even after I had opened my eyes and recovered my senses, it seemed to me that I could still see Azzo’s figure standing before my bed, and that it gradually dissolved into mist and floated out through the door of the room.

U181.text: Very well, young lady! I beg you, Franziska von Fahnenberg, for the sake of your own welfare, as well as for the love you bear your father, whose whole heart is bound up in his only daughter, to weigh my words carefully, and not to interrupt me with questions which I cannot answer until the deed has been accomplished. Your life is in the greatest danger from the illness under which you suffer; indeed, you are inevitably lost unless you carry out what I am about to tell you. I would not have required it of you—indeed, I freely confess that I would have given up all hope of saving you—had I not taken into account your accustomed courage and known the firmness of your will. Now promise me that you will unconditionally do what I tell you. I pledge you my knightly word: it is neither against God nor against the honor of your house, and it is the only means of saving you.

U187.text: You see the open crypt over there! Open the packet; inside are three long iron nails and a hammer. Wait a moment; but as soon as I begin to pray the Credo aloud, with all the strength you possess you must use the hammer to drive first one nail, then the second, and finally the third, vertically through the lid and into the coffin, until each is driven in to its head.

U207.text: It was during my first campaign in Hungary, when through this saber-cut which a valiant Janissary dealt me across the face, and a second wound which I received in the shoulder, I was for a time rendered unfit for combat. I was taken in by a fairly well-to-do family in a small town. It consisted of father, mother, and a daughter of about twenty years of age. The family made its living by serving the wine, which was very good in that region, and the drinking-room was always filled with guests. Although, as I have already said, the family was prosperous, a great sadness nevertheless always prevailed among them, arising from the continual ill health of their only daughter, a very pretty and pious young maiden. The girl had formerly bloomed like a rose, but for several months she had been wasting away until she was little more than a skeleton, without anyone knowing the cause. Every possible effort was made to restore her health, but in vain. As the army was encamped very nearby, it was inevitable that a great many unknown guests of various nations should visit the wine-house. Among them there appeared every evening a man remarkable for his peculiarities, he looked ashen and withered, spoke hardly at all, and whatever he did say was bitter and mocking. What attracted the greatest attention was that, although he always ordered a cup of the best wine and from time to time even raised it to his lips, the cup was invariably found full after the guest had departed—and he came only in the evening by moonlight and never remained longer than an hour!

U208.text: All of that corresponds wonderfully with Knight Azzo’s appearance!

U209.text: The daughter of the house, grew sicker from day to day, without anyone being able to discover any cause, the true origin of her illness, despite every effort made to do so. They consulted not only Christian physicians, but even appealed to prisoners among the heathen peoples, since it is well known that among them there are persons exceedingly familiar with all manner of black-magical practices and strange arcana. It was strange that the maiden continually complained of a dream in which the unknown guest from the wine-house tormented and molested her.

U211.text: One evening, I was sitting over a glass of wine with an old Slavonian who had made many sea voyages to Greece and Turkey, indeed even as far as the New World, when that unknown man entered the room and, as silent as ever, seated himself at the table. The cup passed diligently back and forth between the Slavonian and me, and we became more and more deeply engaged in conversation. He told me about the Turks, how they had impaled Greeks by the dozen like fieldfares; about the Indians of the New World; and how gold there was sometimes said to lie about on the riverbanks in pieces as large as a man’s fist, like pebbles—although he himself had never found such a pebble. I, in turn, told him remarkable things from the little country, as we Silesians like to call our homeland: old stories about Duke Hans of Sagan, how he had allowed his brother Walzer to starve to death at Priebus, how he asked the canons who refused to say Mass upon the bridge at Glogau: ‘Dear sirs, will you sing or spring?’ and other such diverting and agreeable tales. Thus we chatted for an hour and drank a respectable number of tankards. The unknown man, however, had remained silent as usual. He said not a word, merely smiled mockingly from time to time, then paid and made ready to leave. All this had been quietly irritating me, until the annoyance went to my head—and the wine may have done so to some extent as well—so I said to the stranger: ‘Hold there, you tight-lipped guest! Until now you have done nothing but listen, and you have not even emptied your cup. Now you must entertain us with something as well; and if you do not drink your cup dry, we shall take it as an insult.’ ‘Yes!’ shouted the Slavonian. ‘You must stay, talk, and drink!’ And with that he seized the stranger by the shoulder—for although he was no longer young, he was a large man and strong as an oak—in order to force him back into his seat. But the stranger, though thin as a skeleton, with a single movement of his hand hurled the Slavonian into the middle of the room and onto the floor, so that for the first moment he forgot all about getting up. Now I sprang forward to hold the stranger fast. I seized him by the hand, and although the screws of my iron fist were set somewhat less tightly than those of the hand I use now, in the heat of the moment I must nevertheless have gripped him a little strongly; for the stranger, though at first he had glared at me savagely, bent toward me and hissed into my ear: ‘Let me go! From the pressure of your fist I see that you are my brother. Therefore do not prevent me from going in search of my bloody sustenance. I am hungry.’ Astonished by these words, I released him, and before I knew what had happened he was out through the door. Scarcely had I recovered somewhat from my astonishment when I repeated to the Slavonian the words that had remained incomprehensible to me. He was greatly alarmed. I could see that he knew what the matter was, and I pressed him to explain the stranger’s words to me. On the way home he did so. ‘The stranger,’ he said, ‘is a vampire!’

U212.text: What? Then Azzo too would be—

U213.text: It can be no otherwise! He too is one. In any case, however, his infernal craving has now been stilled; he will not return.—But hear the rest.—Since nothing is known of vampires in my homeland, I questioned the Slavonian at length. He said that in Hungary, Carniola, Dalmatia, and Bosnia such infernal spirits were by no means uncommon. They were dead persons who had themselves once served as nourishment for vampires, or who had died in mortal sin or under excommunication, and who, as soon as the moon stood in the sky, rose from their graves and sucked the blood of the living by night. A person who served a vampire as nourishment in this fashion would waste away and slowly sicken toward the grave, and nothing could save him unless the vampire could be bound fast within its grave. This could be accomplished only by nailing it fast in its coffin with three iron nails, under the protection of the Most High, at the hour when day and night divide.

U219.text: You can now imagine, noble young lady, how alarmed I was by your condition when I arrived. Everything that you or Bertha told me had aroused my attention, and when I saw Azzo, I no longer had any doubt that he was a vampire. His appearance, his behavior, were exactly like those of the unknown man of whom I told you. The encounter with Franz finally gave me complete certainty. Since, from the account of your adventure near the ruins, I could determine where Azzo’s grave was to be sought, I had no doubt that you could be saved, provided only that I could persuade you to take part in your own deliverance. I did not consider it advisable to reveal the full truth to you, because I believed your bodily strength already so impaired that a description of what lay before you might perhaps have exhausted it completely before the necessary deed could be performed. For that reason I arranged everything as it came to pass.

U223.text: I do not know! That very night the district was alarmed by the Turks, and we were obliged to depart; I never heard anything of her again.
